{/* ===================================================== 1. THE BACKSTORY & THE REAL PROBLEM ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("01 · THE BACKSTORY")}

Understanding the business and the legacy app

When I joined as the sole product designer, the client had an existing web portal that dealerships and regional managers dreaded using. Everyone was keeping their real numbers in massive, disjointed Excel sheets.

Before jumping into Figma, I had to understand where the data was actually coming from. Dealerships handle dozens of interconnected business lines:

Equipment Data

Tracking machine populations across C&I (Construction & Infrastructure) and heavy Mining machinery, warranty schedules, and uptime.

Parts & Service Revenue

Monitoring parts & lubes inventory turnover, bay throughput, customer service agreements (CSA), and quarterly revenue targets.

People & Facilities

Technician competence certifications (SCL/TCL/LCL), training calendarization, and capital investment for EV tools and showroom growth.

The Real Pain Point:

The old app just dumped raw database tables onto the screen. If a dealer's first-time fix rate was falling, managers couldn't tell whether it was caused by delayed parts shipments or a shortage of certified technicians. Everything had to be cross-referenced by hand during monthly reviews.

{/* ===================================================== 2. HOW I DID USER RESEARCH ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("02 · HOW I DID RESEARCH")}

Practical discovery with stakeholders & users

Because this was a complex enterprise tool, I didn't do generic surveys. Instead, I did focused, practical discovery sessions:

1. Sitting with Stakeholders & PMs

I sat with product managers and business stakeholders to walk through the Business Requirement Documents (BRDs). I asked simple, direct questions: "What numbers do managers look at on day one of the month? Which numbers trigger an urgent call?"

2. Auditing the Old Sheets & Screen Flows

I collected the actual spreadsheets that regional managers used before their monthly dealer meetings. I highlighted columns that were checked every time versus columns that were purely background records.

3. Identifying the 3 Core Roles

I realized three distinct groups used the tool: Dealer Principals (care about high-level quarterly targets & revenue), Operations Managers (care about daily service bays, parts, and machine uptime), and Training Managers (care about technician licenses expiring).

4. The Big Insight: Connect Data to Action

Seeing a bad number was not enough. If an audit found a broken tool or missing EV safety equipment, the user had to open Outlook and email someone. The new design had to let them turn an issue into an assigned action item right from the screen.

{/* ===================================================== 3. WIREFRAMING & CLIENT APPROVAL ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("03 · WIREFRAMES & APPROVALS")}

Wireframing first, getting client sign-off

I never design final UI in colors right away. For every module, I started with low-fidelity wireframes in FigJam and Figma. I reviewed these directly with the client and stakeholders to agree on information hierarchy before touching typography or styling.

{/* Interactive Wireframe vs High-Fi Switcher */}

Client feedback during low-fi review: "We don't need 20 charts on the main page. Give us the 3 core numbers on top, and put the dealer list right below with an immediate action button." That directly shaped the final UI.

{/* ===================================================== 4. AUTO LAYOUT & DESIGN SYSTEM ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("04 · AUTO LAYOUT & COMPONENTS")}

Auto layout, components & design consistency

Because I had to design over 20 submodules (PDP, Equipment, Uptime, Dealer Investment, Competence, DFHM, Action Planner, etc.), doing one-off screen designs was out of the question.

I built a clean, scalable component system in Figma with 100% Auto Layout so every card, table row, and modal could resize cleanly:

Auto Layout Everything

Headers, toolbars, and nested table cells were built with Auto Layout so developers could see exact padding, gap tokens, and resizing behavior.

Reusable UI Library

Created reusable components for KPI cards, table rows, filter chips, breadcrumbs, status badges, and side-drawers used across all 20+ modules.

Strict Color Tokens

Standardized status colors: Emerald for targets met, Amber for pending SLAs (14-day alert), and Rose exclusively for audit non-conformance blocks.

{/* ===================================================== 5. MODULES, DASHBOARD & CHARTS ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("05 · MODULES & CHARTS")}

Designing the modules, then the executive dashboard

I designed each operational module first to make sure the detailed tables and workflows worked. Then, I tackled the most important piece: the executive dashboard and charts.

Regional managers didn't want to click through 10 pages just to see if their zone was doing well. I synthesized the data from all modules into high-level visual charts:

Quarterly Trend Trajectory Curves

Replaced static PDF monthly bars with an interactive trend chart showing actual performance against the regional target line, so managers instantly see if they are falling behind mid-quarter.

Side-Drawer Row Expansion

Rather than overloading tables with 30 columns, clicking any dealer row slides open a clean side drawer displaying their machine population breakdown (C&I vs Mining), facility audit checklist, and open tickets.

Action Planner Integration

Every chart and table has a direct "Create Action Ticket" shortcut that feeds straight into the Kanban board, creating mutual accountability between dealership heads and regional consultants.

{/* ===================================================== 6. DEVELOPER HANDOFF ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("06 · DEVELOPER HANDOFF")}

Developer handoff & frontend collaboration

Because of my frontend background, I know that designs often break during implementation if edge cases aren't thought through. I treated developer handoff as a core deliverable:

Documented States & Edge Cases

Prepared Figma handoff specs showing default, hover, active, loading skeletons, empty data states, and error handling for every component.

Virtualization & Table Scrolling

Specified sticky frozen columns for dealer IDs and worked with engineers to ensure tables with 1,400+ rows rendered smoothly without lag.

Responsive Breakpoints

Field consultants conduct workshop audits on iPads and tablets. I created adapted responsive layouts so checklists were touch-friendly on 11-inch screens.

Ongoing Dev Syncs & QA

Held weekly design-dev review syncs during sprints to test built components against the Figma designs and fix visual discrepancies early.

{/* ===================================================== 7. KEY LEARNINGS ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("07 · REFLECTION")}

What I learned as the sole product designer

Owning Volvo Partner Connect 2.0 end-to-end taught me that great enterprise product design is about untangling complexity. Anyone can make a pretty landing page, but building a multi-module platform where real people manage multi-million dollar dealer operations requires:

  • Domain Empathy First: Understanding how dealers make money and how equipment gets serviced matters more than surface-level aesthetic trends.
  • Communication with Stakeholders: Low-fi wireframes and honest feedback sessions save weeks of re-work compared to presenting finished UI out of nowhere.
  • Speaking Developer Language: Understanding tokens, auto layout, and frontend constraints creates mutual trust between design and engineering.
